WHY IT HAS TO EXIST

The cost of bad quality is enormous.
The tools to catch it went enterprise.

Quality escapes are one of manufacturing’s largest quiet costs, and small factories carry them with the fewest defences, because the AI inspection industry built its products around customers with ML teams.

F·01

Quality costs real margin

Industry estimates associated with ASQ place the cost of poor quality at 15–20% of sales for many manufacturers: scrap, rework, returns and the customers who never come back.

F·02

The adoption cliff

Eurostat data shows around 30% of large EU enterprises using AI against roughly 7% of small ones. In quality inspection, that gap maps directly to who ships defects and who catches them.

F·03

Projects, not products

Conventional vision systems arrive as integration projects: consultants, custom training, months of tuning per part variant. By some industry estimates most AI projects never reach production, a risk small firms cannot underwrite.

F·04

The knowledge is already in the room

Most factories have someone who can spot the bad part at a glance. That expertise leaves with retirement and shift changes. That person should be able to teach it to a camera, directly.

For the factory
without an AI department.

The SME production line

The design customer runs one to five lines, employs no data scientist, and lives or dies on reputation with a handful of key buyers. The system must earn its place with that operation: taught in an afternoon, useful in a week, priced like equipment.

NO ML TEAM1–5 LINESREPUTATION-CRITICALEQUIPMENT-PRICED

Quality leads

High-mix producers

WHAT IT CHANGES

Show it examples.
Confirm its calls. That’s the method.

The system is assistive by design: it flags, a human disposes. Every confirmation is also training data, so the detector sharpens as a side effect of the line running.

Escapes caught at the line.

Every unit inspected at production speed, suspects flagged for human decision before they reach a box, a truck, or a customer.

Taught by example.

New part, new defect class, new variant: taught by example from the floor, in-session. The six-month vision project collapses into an afternoon.

Quality memory built.

Every flagged unit archived with image and disposition: the factory’s defect history becomes searchable evidence for audits, claims and process fixes.

THE MECHANICS

Edge box at the line.
Learning loop on the floor.

Cameras over the line, an edge unit beside it, a teaching screen in the quality office, and a training loop that lives inside the factory. Product images never need to leave the building.

Every VF system runs on the harness stack, is steered by the Helmsman engine and is watched from a command dashboard.

LAYER 1

The capture layer

Industrial cameras positioned over the line, triggered per unit or continuously: commodity hardware where possible, matched to line speed and part size.

LAYER 2

The edge core

Detection models running on an on-site unit at line speed. On-premise by default: the factory’s parts, defects and volumes stay the factory’s business.

LAYER 3

The teaching loop

Example-based training driven by quality staff: label, correct, confirm. Few-shot techniques mean useful detection from dozens of examples, converging with every shift worked.

LAYER 4

The quality surface

The flag queue for dispositions, trend dashboards per line and variant, and the archived defect record, exportable for audits and customer quality agreements.

One line proven,
then every floor like it.

PLANNED
QUESTIONS

Asked.
Answered.

Do I need an ML engineer?

No. The person who knows what a defect looks like becomes the teacher: your quality lead labels examples on a screen, corrects the system’s calls and watches it converge on their eye. Few-shot techniques mean useful detection from dozens of examples, so a new part, defect class or variant is taught in a session.

Does it reject parts on its own?

No. The system is assistive by design: it flags, a human disposes. Every unit is inspected at production speed and suspects are queued for human decision before they reach a box, a truck or a customer. Every confirmation is also training data, so the detector sharpens as a side effect of the line running.

Where do the product images go?

They stay in the building. Detection models run on an on-site edge unit at line speed, on-premise by default, so the factory’s parts, defects and volumes remain the factory’s business. Flagged units are archived with image and disposition as a searchable defect record, exportable for audits and customer quality agreements.

Which factories is it for?

The SME production line: one to five lines, no data scientist, living on reputation with a handful of key buyers. Quality leads, plant managers, contract manufacturers who need documented inspection as a sales asset, and high-mix producers with short runs and frequent changeovers, where teaching a new variant must take minutes.

When does it ship?

Self-Training QC Vision is in build. The first line phase runs pilot deployments on real SME lines: capture setup, edge detection and the teaching loop proven with working quality leads on their actual defect classes. High-mix workflows and multi-site views follow, then general availability with equipment-style pricing and MES and ERP connectors. VF chooses pilot lines from the interest list.
